newsitem.title: LEBANON: Low Lebanon vote, Hizbollah could lose ground.
newsitem.headline: Low Lebanon vote, Hizbollah could lose ground.

text.p: Low turnout on Sunday in the final round of voting in the eastern Bekaa valley appeared to threaten the pro-Iranian Hizbollah with a new setback in Lebanon's parliamentary election.

Six-and-a-half hours after the polls opened, only 11.5 percent of the 410,000 voters had cast their ballots, Interior Minister Michel al-Murr said. Polling stations were due to close at 5:00 p.m. (1400 GMT) and results were expected on Monday or Tuesday.
The Bekaa was electing the last 23 members to the 128-member parliament after voting in Mount Lebanon, the north, Beirut and the south on the past four Sundays.
The Lebanese Association for the Democracy of Elections (LADE), an independent watchdog, reported thousands of irregularities in the poll. It reported widespread abuses in the earlier rounds.

A pro-government list including six ministers, several parliamentary deputies and candidates of Hizbollah and the secular Amal, Lebanon's two main rival Shi'ite Moslem movements, was expected to win most of the seats.
It was challenged by a 10-man leftist ticket headed by communist party leader Farouk Dharouje and a six-man list of independents.
The low turnout appeared to threaten the chances of a Maronite Christian and a Sunni Moslem candidate that Hizbollah (Party of God) was backing on the list, observers said.
Hizbollah lost two of its eight parliamentary seats in earlier rounds and losses by two supporters in the Bekaa would be another damaging political blow.
Hizbollah's Sunni supporter could lose because he was facing popular Sunni rivals on other lists, local observers said.
Christians, who total over 25 percent of Bekaa voters, were either refusing to vote or were crossing Hizbollah and its supporters off their ballot papers.
Reporters at polling stations saw many people holding ballot papers with Hizbollah candidates crossed off.
"Hizbollah candidates are being deleted. We still don't know how widely practised this has been but there is evident deletion of our candidates' names," Hizbollah deputy Khodr Tleis told reporters.
Local observers said Bekaa Christians were angry because a Maronite Christian on the pro-government list was chosen by Hizbollah under an election deal brokered by Syria.
They were also showing dislike for President Elias Hrawi, a pro-Syrian Maronite from the Bekaa town of Zahle. Hrawi's son Roy failed to win election in Zahle at the last elections in 1992.
Hizbollah sources said the pro-Iranian movement was holding back its voters until the last minute for tactical reasons.
It was due under election deals engineered by Syria to have seven deputies and two supporters in parliament compared with eight deputies and four supporters before.

Syria has 35,000 troops in Lebanon and a large presence in the Bekaa. Local politicians say it intervened to engineer the makeup of the pro-government list to prevent politicians it dislikes from being elected and to avert an open fight between Amal and Hizbollah in the predominantly Shi'ite region.
The Bekaa is a stronghold of Hizbollah, which has military training camps in the valley for its guerrillas who are fighting Israeli troops in a south Lebanon border strip.
But it has only three members and two supporters on the pro-government list. Amal has one member and one supporter.
